logline: A brilliant first-year attorney with autism navigates a Seoul law firm, the courtroom, and the social rules everyone else learned without a manual.

bollymeter.basis: 100% on Rotten Tomatoes (11 critics); IMDb 8.5; sixth most-viewed non-English drama in Netflix history at time of airing; critics converged on Park Eun-bin's performance and the show's balance between procedural warmth and genuine social commentary.

pull_quotes.text: Park Eun-bin delivers one of the great K-drama performances - precise, layered, never reducing Woo Young-woo to quirk.

seasons.review_body: Extraordinary Attorney Woo cracked the global Netflix top 10 non-English shows and stayed there for weeks, and the 100% Rotten Tomatoes score explains why: this is a case-of-the-week show where every case illuminates the lead character's particular way of seeing the world. The show's central gamble is Park Eun-bin, and she does not miss a single beat across 16 episodes. Critics flagged her performance as the rare portrayal of autism on screen that is rigorous rather than symbolic - the whales, the palindromes, the specific social calculations are all character not shorthand. The romantic subplot between Woo Young-woo and Lee Jun-ho became one of K-drama's most discussed relationships of 2022, partly for its slowness, partly for its gentleness. The show's one persistent criticism: individual case resolutions can feel formulaic in the middle stretch.

episode_reviews.title: Woo Young-woo, Extraordinary and Peculiar
episode_reviews.review_body: Extraordinary Attorney Woo's premiere aired June 29, 2022 on ENA and immediately began the run to the Netflix global top 10 that would define the show's commercial story. Writer Moon Ji-won's central decision was the one the premiere honours completely: to establish Woo Young-woo as a fully realised person - with her own history, humour, and internal logic - before deploying her as a legal prodigy. Park Eun-bin arrived with the character already fully formed, and the premiere gave the performance room to breathe across its runtime rather than rushing to the courtroom. The case - a will contest involving a family dispute - was selected with evident care: it allowed the premiere to demonstrate the specific quality of Woo Young-woo's legal reasoning without requiring the audience to already know the character. Rotten Tomatoes recorded a 100 percent approval score from critics on the first season, with the consensus noting 'one of the warmest, sharpest drama premieres in recent Korean television.' The revolving door gag at the law firm's entrance - which the premiere introduces and which the series returns to with accumulated meaning - was immediately isolated as the episode's signature formal choice.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The pilot spends its entire runtime establishing Woo Young-woo as a complete person before establishing her as a legal prodigy - the order of priorities is revealing. Her first day at the firm is observed with patience and wit. The case involves a will contest and whales; the latter connection to the lead makes perfect internal sense.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The revolving door sequence - Woo's first arrival at the firm becomes a recurring gag that accrues meaning across the season.

critic_note.text: One of the warmest, sharpest drama premieres in recent Korean television.

episode_reviews.title: Extraordinary Attorney Woo Returns
episode_reviews.review_body: Extraordinary Attorney Woo Episode 13 aired August 4, 2022 and was identified by critics and domestic viewers as the moment the series moved decisively beyond case-of-the-week pleasures into something more architecturally ambitious. The episode - the first of the show's return arc after a structural pause - placed Woo Young-woo in a professional situation where her extraordinary cognitive abilities were necessary but not sufficient: the case demanded the institutional support and interpersonal trust she had been quietly building across twelve prior episodes. Writer Moon Ji-won's structural intelligence is most visible here: the episode's legal narrative and the personal narrative about Woo's relationship with Jun-ho converge at a point that both plots had been approaching from different directions. The Rotten Tomatoes critics consensus noted the episode as 'proof the show is more than its charming premise.' The courtroom argument sequence that connected the legal case to something deeply personal in Woo's history was identified as the show's most-clipped scene on social media across the ENA and Netflix broadcast windows, and drew specific attention in South Korean press reviews for the formal precision with which Park Eun-bin calibrated the transition from professional argumentation to personal revelation.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The penultimate arc's emotional peak - the case here forces Woo Young-woo into a situation that tests whether her extraordinary mind is sufficient without the institutional support she has been quietly building. The professional and personal threads converge with unusual elegance.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Woo's courtroom argument that connects her case to something deeply personal - the scene that became the show's most clipped moment online.

critic_note.text: The episode that proves the show is more than its charming premise.
